anchors.quote: on the first pass probably about 30 seconds

claim_en: On the first pass the recruiter spends about 30 seconds on a CV.

anchors.quote: the recruiter isn't really trying to understand the entire career at that point they're trying to really establish whether that's enough relevant experience to justify carrying on reading

claim_en: On the first pass the recruiter is not trying to understand the whole career, only whether there is enough relevant experience to justify reading on.

anchors.quote: typically I'd look at the most recent experience first if it's in date order um you know what you've been doing what technologies you've been using how closely does that match with the problem that the company is trying to solve
I'd scan for recent and relevant experience

claim_en: The recruiter typically reads the most recent experience first and judges how closely its work and technologies match the problem the company is trying to solve.

anchors.quote: if I can't see a technical fit on page one it's you know it's difficult to keep going when you'got a sea of applications to get through

claim_en: When the recruiter cannot see a technical fit on page one, it is difficult to keep reading with a sea of applications to get through.

anchors.quote: the recruiter would review inbound applications or then actively search for somebody through like LinkedIn or a job board or their network

claim_en: Recruiters find candidates by two routes: reviewing inbound applications, or actively searching through LinkedIn, job boards or their network.

anchors.quote: if the profile looks relevant the next step would usually be a phone screening

claim_en: If a profile looks relevant, the next step is usually a phone screening.

anchors.quote: I wasn't really looking for somebody to repeat their CV on that phone screening i wanted to know whether they could back up whatever was written in their CV you know what was the problem what did you personally do what changed because of your work

claim_en: On the phone screening the recruiter did not want candidates to repeat the CV but to back up what it says: the problem, what they personally did and what changed because of their work.

anchors.quote: I'd then decide which candidates to introduce to the hiring manager so then what that means is that the recruiter must be able to explain internally why you're worth meeting
we have to justify why a person is right and on that first phone screening that's why it's important to understand not just the tech you've worked on but what problems you solved

claim_en: The recruiter decides which candidates to introduce to the hiring manager and must be able to justify internally why each is worth meeting, so needs to understand the problems the candidate solved, not just the tech.

anchors.quote: i never relied heavily on an ATS to make any kind of hiring decisions
rather than expecting a system to decide whether someone was good or not

claim_en: In their own experience the recruiter never relied heavily on an ATS for hiring decisions and scanned applications personally rather than expecting a system to judge candidates.

anchors.quote: the main exception was any kind of hard requirement so like security clearance would often be needed you know you'd need the ATS to filter anybody that wasn't SC eligible

claim_en: The recruiter used the ATS mainly to filter out applicants who failed a hard requirement such as security clearance eligibility.

anchors.quote: candidates definitely shouldn't ignore key words because you know recruiters still need to find them
you should definitely optimize your CV to be found

claim_en: Candidates should not ignore keywords, because recruiters still need to find their CVs.

anchors.quote: they also shouldn't write a CV for a robot and then it makes it unreadable for a human we still need to be able to like understand your job the problems you've solved um rather than just DevOps Kubernetes Python
optimize your CV to be found but write it to be understood

claim_en: Candidates should not write the CV for a robot so that it becomes unreadable for a human; the reader needs to understand the job and the problems solved, not a string of buzzwords.

anchors.quote: heavily relying on AI to do a lot of the filtering to do a lot of the booking and all those sorts of things is is a bit of a recipe for disaster because you still want that human to be able to understand context

claim_en: In the recruiter's view, relying heavily on AI to filter applicants is a recipe for disaster, because a human is still needed to understand context the job spec does not state.

anchors.quote: technical fit is is immediately obvious on page one if I'm recruiting for like a React engineer I shouldn't have to search through pages to find the React experience
make the match easy to see and never expect a recruiter to to work it out for you
look at the first page of your CV does it clearly show the skills that are required by those roles
make your technical fit obvious on page one

claim_en: What makes the recruiter stop and pay attention is a technical fit that is immediately obvious on page one; a recruiter hiring for a stack should not have to search through pages to find it.

anchors.quote: candidate had strong full stack foundations but the client needed uh react and the profile showed view much more clearly um so the person is probably great probably very capable but the evidence that the hiring manager needed wasn't visible enough

claim_en: From the employer side the recruiter recently saw a capable full stack candidate whose profile showed Vue more clearly than the React the client needed, so the evidence the hiring manager needed was not visible enough.

anchors.quote: the stronger candidates also explain context
don't simply give me a list of technologies tell me what you're building what problem you're solving your personal contribution and the result as well

listing technologies without explaining the project or or your contribution so um Java AWS Kubernetes tells me very little you know what did you build what was difficult what did you own what improved
are you showing achievements and problem solved or like just merely listing responsibilities
show the projects that you'delivered don't just show that you know a technology um show the problems you've solved

claim_en: Do not just list technologies or responsibilities; say what was built, what problem was solved, the personal contribution and the result.

anchors.quote: the first one I would definitely say is length most CVs don't need to document every task from every do job someone has ever had

claim_en: Length is the first of the biggest CV mistakes the recruiter sees: most CVs do not need to document every task from every job.

anchors.quote: the second is poor presentation i think a recruiter or anybody looking at your CV you know the recipient on the other end needs to be able to navigate the document quickly so like fancy graphics they're not really necessary at that point it's more about clarity

claim_en: Poor presentation is the second biggest CV mistake: the reader must be able to navigate the document quickly, and fancy graphics are not necessary; clarity matters.

anchors.quote: a genuine concern that I would have would be somebody who had been out of work for a long period but couldn't show any learning or projects or effort to remain current

claim_en: A genuine concern for the recruiter is a candidate out of work for a long period who cannot show any learning, projects or effort to stay current.

anchors.quote: the gap itself isn't really the problem to be honest with you because everybody has gaps in their employment but it's what the person did

claim_en: For the recruiter an employment gap is not the problem in itself, since everybody has gaps; what matters is what the person did during it.

anchors.quote: I met a head of engineering who's been out of work for 18 months He is putting himself out there on LinkedIn he's going to events he's networking he's building side projects at home
this is all um searchable on his LinkedIn so even though he's out of work he's still current

claim_en: The recruiter cites a head of engineering out of work for 18 months who stays current through LinkedIn activity, events, networking and side projects that are searchable on LinkedIn, and says such things make a big difference.

anchors.quote: I don't think there's a a right number but I would say maximum absolute maximum five pages

claim_en: There is no right number of pages, but five pages is the absolute maximum.

anchors.quote: somebody with 10 to 15 years experience you can definitely have five pages to capture your your experience

claim_en: With 10 to 15 years of experience a CV can be up to five pages.

anchors.quote: if you're like two or three years into your career you're not going to feel five pages and that's fine if your CV is two or three pages great

claim_en: Two or three years into a career, a CV of two or three pages is fine.

value.condition: two or three years into a career

anchors.quote: a one pager probably wouldn't capture enough and also I think when you receive a onepage CV I'm not sure the kind of message that that sends to the recruiter

claim_en: A one page CV probably does not capture enough and sends an unclear message to the recruiter.

anchors.quote: I guess between between like two and five would be a good number

claim_en: Between two and five pages is a good CV length.

anchors.quote: page one you know You can have a section where you list your technologies because you know you want to be able to show whoever's reading your CV that you'got the required skill set

claim_en: Page one can have a section listing technologies, to show the reader the required skill set for the job.

anchors.quote: you don't just want a bunch of technologies listed there if they're already on page one great let the recruiter assume that you've used those technologies across different projects
you can like sprinkle in the kind of tech you use
don't then list every technology on every project
you don't need to list every single technology that you worked on in every single project

claim_en: Do not list a bunch of technologies under each position when they are already on page one; sprinkle the tech into the description of the work instead of listing every technology on every project.

anchors.quote: under each project and each career uh entry you should put you know the topic so fintech or financial services or healthcare this was the problem this is what we were solving these were our end customers

claim_en: Under each project and role entry, state the domain (such as fintech or healthcare), the problem being solved and the end customers.

anchors.quote: first check whether you're genuinely applying for roles that fit your experience

claim_en: A candidate who gets no interviews should first check whether they are genuinely applying for roles that fit their experience.

anchors.quote: they just go apply for everything that's going to do you no good whatsoever
more applications probably aren't the solution if you're applying to hundreds of jobs and then hearing nothing
don't make the mistake of thinking that applying for more jobs automatically improves your chances it's not necessarily a volume game

claim_en: Applying for everything, for example with AI, does no good; more applications are not the solution when hundreds of applications get no response.

anchors.quote: is your location and right to work position obvious
remove uncertainty wherever you can so be clear about your right to work your location your availability
be transparent about your location and visa situation

claim_en: Make the location and right to work position obvious; be clear and transparent about location, visa situation and availability.

anchors.quote: if you know someone in the industry potentially ask them to review it for you because it's always good to have another set of eyes on what you've written
ask somebody to have a look at your your CV for you um I think it's easy to become too close to your own CV and assume other people make connections that aren't necessarily obvious

claim_en: Ask someone, ideally in the industry, to review the CV, because authors are too close to their own CV and assume readers make connections that are not obvious.

anchors.quote: diagnose the point of failure no interviews usually means targeting positioning or visibility

claim_en: When applications bring no interviews, diagnose the point of failure: it usually lies in targeting, positioning or visibility.

anchors.quote: LinkedIn and networking and referrals they can actually be a bit more important than the CV because they help you escape the application queue

claim_en: In the recruiter's opinion LinkedIn, networking and referrals can be more important than the CV, because they help the candidate escape the application queue.

anchors.quote: if somebody went out of their way to send me a thoughtful and relevant message I would notice it
a short message explaining why their background matched my role or my company um that's powerful

claim_en: The recruiter notices a short, thoughtful message explaining why the sender's background matches the role or company, unlike a generic request for a job.

anchors.quote: a referral transfers some of the trust as well um it doesn't guarantee an interview or a job obviously but a hiring manager or somebody can look at your profile a bit more carefully

claim_en: A referral transfers some trust: it does not guarantee an interview, but a hiring manager looks at the profile more carefully.

anchors.quote: a lot of the placements that that I would make in my early career all came from referrals i would say probably as much as like 70%

claim_en: In the recruiter's early career about 70 percent of placements came from referrals.

anchors.quote: the more you're putting yourself out there networking and speaking to people whether that's on LinkedIn or in real life events you're just going to get referred

claim_en: The more a candidate networks, on LinkedIn or at real life events, the more referrals they get.

anchors.quote: I personally wouldn't bother with a traditional cover letter unless obviously like you just said they were specifically asking for one

claim_en: The recruiter would not bother with a traditional cover letter unless the employer specifically asks for one.

anchors.quote: i would rather see three or four strong sentences at the top of a CV explaining who you are what you specialize in and why you're a fit for that type of opportunity
if you're applying for 50 jobs you're going to have to tailor that to 50 applications but it's much better to do across three or four sentences than an entire cover letter

claim_en: Instead of a cover letter, put three or four strong sentences at the top of the CV saying who you are, what you specialize in and why you fit, tailored to each application.

anchors.quote: if you're changing careers if you're relocating or you need to explain something unusual a short tailored note can really help you don't need a whole page cover letter

claim_en: When changing careers, relocating or explaining something unusual, a short tailored note can help; a whole page cover letter is not needed.

anchors.quote: a generic page describing how passionate and hardworking you are it adds very little
I want to see something that's like personal like you've done your research you've looked at the job you've looked at the company you've seen our values

claim_en: A generic page about being passionate and hardworking adds very little; anything written should be personal and show research into the job, the company, its values and mission.

anchors.quote: I'd rather see that than a cover letter that probably wouldn't get read

claim_en: In the recruiter's view a traditional cover letter probably would not get read.
